thread: Follow a thread from the garden to the mill and into the museum: the swarm begins among fibre and dye plants, passes through spinning and weaving machinery, and emerges among finished textiles and silkworm collections.

candidates.name: Lund University Botanical Garden
candidates.why: Economic plants include fibre crops and indigo; outdoor beds and greenhouses offer a varied population of leaves, roots, seeds, and dye-bearing plants.

candidates.name: National Museum of Science and Technology of Catalonia
candidates.why: Its former woollen mill holds carding and spinning machinery, looms, boilers, a steam engine, and the tools of dyeing and finishing.

candidates.name: State Silk Museum
candidates.why: Silkworms, cocoons, silk textiles, historic dyes, and a specialist library turn the thread into a collection of living and crafted forms.

candidates.name: LWL Museum Textilwerk
candidates.why: A spinning mill and weaving mill contain spindles, looms, workshop tools, fabric samples, and historic clothing.

candidates.name: The George Washington University Museum and The Textile Museum
candidates.why: Rugs, woven and dyed textiles, and textile-care resources offer patterns, materials, and techniques from many regions.

candidates.name: Ethnographic Museum in Belgrade
candidates.why: Its collections include looms and implements for processing fibre, alongside regional costumes, household objects, and crafts.

candidates.name: TextielMuseum
candidates.why: Historic machinery, textile art, design, and the working TextielLab offer a route from threads to experimental woven surfaces.

candidates.name: Trowbridge Museum
candidates.why: A rare spinning jenny, woollen cloth samples, mill tools, and local costume trace the making and wearing of cloth.

candidates.name: Textilmuseum St.Gallen
candidates.why: Silk fragments, embroidery, pattern books, and a textile library offer intricate forms and surfaces for the swarm to inhabit.
